title: Start reading the Quran
whyMatters: The Quran is the word of Allah, revealed to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) over 23 years. As a Muslim it is where you go first for guidance, comfort, and sense. Reading it works on you spiritually as much as intellectually. Many Muslims describe a settled kind of peace when they read or listen to it. You do not need Arabic to get something out of the Quran. Start where you are and let it talk to you.

exactActions.text: Get a Quran with an English translation
subSteps: Look for a translation you can actually read. Common choices are 'The Clear Quran' by Dr. Mustafa Khattab and 'The Gracious Quran' by Ahmad Zaki Hammad.
Many masjids give free copies to new Muslims, so ask.
You can also use a Quran app like Quran.com or the Al-Quran app, which give you the Arabic text, transliteration, and several translations.
Having both is ideal: the book for sitting down with, the app for everywhere else.
Surah Al-Fatiha (Chapter 1): the opening prayer you recite in every salah. Read its meaning slowly.
Surah Al-Ikhlas (Chapter 112): a short declaration of Allah's oneness, four verses long.
Surah Al-Falaq (Chapter 113) and Surah An-Nas (Chapter 114): two short chapters about asking Allah for protection.
Surah Al-Kawthar (Chapter 108): the shortest chapter in the Quran, three verses.
These chapters at the back of the Quran are where most Muslims start memorizing.
Start with five minutes a day. Doing it regularly matters more than doing a lot.
Pick a regular time. After Fajr and just before bed are the usual choices.
Read the Arabic if you can, then the English translation.
If the Arabic is out of reach for now, reading the translation on its own is completely valid.
Keep a small notebook for the verses that stay with you.
Hearing it recited well does something to you even when you cannot follow the Arabic.
Search for reciters like Mishary Rashid Alafasy, Abdul Rahman Al-Sudais, or Omar Hisham Al-Arabi on YouTube or a Quran app.
Listen on your commute, while you cook, or as you wind down at night.
Reading along while you listen helps your pronunciation and keeps your attention on it.
Begin with Surah Al-Ikhlas, which is four short verses.
Read, listen, and repeat one verse at a time until it sticks.
Once Al-Ikhlas is solid, move to Al-Falaq, then An-Nas.
These chapters get used in prayer, so learning them improves your salah right away.
There is no rush. Some people learn a chapter in a day and others take a month. Both are fine.

obstacles.solution: Most converts cannot read Arabic at the start, and that is fine. Begin with an English translation. Many apps and printed Qurans include transliteration, which is Arabic written in English letters, to help you with the sounds. If you want the script itself, there are beginner courses built for adults. Reading the Quran in translation is fully valid in the meantime and worth doing for its own sake.

obstacles.problem: I don't understand what I'm reading
obstacles.solution: The Quran is layered, and lifelong Muslims spend decades on its meanings. Use a translation with short commentary (tafsir) to fill in the context. 'The Clear Quran' has useful footnotes. There are also short tafsir videos that walk through a chapter in plain language. Understanding arrives over years, so do not expect to hold all of it now.

Tie the reading to something you already do, like your morning prayer or your lunch break. Set a gentle reminder. Keep the book or the app within reach, because out of sight really does mean out of mind. One verse on a busy day still counts. What matters is not letting the habit stop altogether.

obstacles.problem: I feel overwhelmed by the size of the Quran
obstacles.solution: There are 114 chapters, and nobody expects you to read them front to back right now. Start with the short ones at the back (Juz Amma, the 30th section). Plenty of Muslims read through the Quran across months or years. Some finish it during Ramadan, but treat that as a later goal. For now you are building a relationship with it, not completing it.

obstacles.problem: Some verses seem confusing or harsh
obstacles.solution: Context does most of the work in the Quran. Verses that read as difficult often make sense once you know the situation they were revealed into, which is what tafsir (commentary) is for. Take the ones that trouble you to a knowledgeable Muslim or an imam. Asking is what a sincere seeker does, not a sign of weak faith.

tinyVersion: If you do one thing, download a Quran app and read Surah Al-Fatiha in translation. Sit with what it says. That is a good start.
unlocksNext: As the Quran gets more familiar, you are ready for the practical guidance it gives about daily life, starting with halal and haram.
